text:
**Review Result**

Score: 6.5/10. The repo is small, readable, and has a useful test suite: `pytest -q` passes 61 tests. I did not find obvious command injection or SQL injection. The main problem is correctness under real operational data, especially out-of-order snapshots and report behavior.

I would not approve this as-is.

**Findings**

High: [jobwatch/db.py](/work/jobwatch/db.py:31) treats every unrecognized state as terminal, so a later lower-ranked legitimate update can be skipped permanently.

High: [jobwatch/db.py](/work/jobwatch/db.py:70) only compares lifecycle rank before upsert; older same-rank snapshots can overwrite newer elapsed/end/state data.

Medium: [jobwatch/cli.py](/work/jobwatch/cli.py:121) and [jobwatch/db.py](/work/jobwatch/db.py:52) make report/top commands create a missing DB and return empty success, masking typoed paths or lost data.

Medium: [jobwatch/parser.py](/work/jobwatch/parser.py:148) accepts negative `AllocCPUS` and GPU TRES counts, producing negative resource-hour reports.

Medium: [jobwatch/parser.py](/work/jobwatch/parser.py:152) stores empty user/partition/exit-code fields without validation, causing misleading grouped reports.

Medium: [jobwatch/reports.py](/work/jobwatch/reports.py:14) compares ISO timestamp text lexicographically; timezone-offset inputs can filter/sort incorrectly unless timestamps are normalized to a common representation.

Low: [jobwatch/parser.py](/work/jobwatch/parser.py:176) strips only `\n`, so CRLF input rejects the header or preserves trailing `\r` in fields.

Low: [jobwatch/db.py](/work/jobwatch/db.py:13) has no indexes for reference-time/report queries, so usage/failure/top reports become full-table scans as the accounting database grows.

Estimated rewrite/significant-change size: about 120 lines, mostly update-ordering logic, DB open modes, parser validation, timestamp normalization, indexes, and focused tests.
